rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Table 2/Fig. 7 report the authors' own four-year field deployment (2017-2020) of an IoT DSS using infrared radiometers at two Idaho vineyards, with CWSI validated against measured LWP and fASW.
rows.notes: The study uses in-situ thermal infrared radiometers (not imagery) to compute a daily CWSI and shows it correlates with LWP and fASW and that managers used it daily for irrigation decisions (Sections 3.2, 4.4). It does not identify spatial stress zones (sensors on a single row), and reports no yield or grape quality data, so the claimed effect of maintaining yield and quality is not tested; only the precondition (stress monitoring informing irrigation) is supported.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report original field data from two vineyards over four seasons (CWSI from radiometers, LWP by pressure chamber, soil moisture, irrigation amounts).
rows.notes: The study combines CWSI with weather sensor data, but uses point infrared radiometers rather than thermal imagery, does not map stress zones, and reports no grape quality or yield outcomes. It shows CWSI tracks vine water status (Fig. 7, Fig. 8) and guided manager irrigation decisions, which is a precondition for the claimed preservation of quality and yield, not evidence of it.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own sensor, LWP and irrigation measurements over 2017-2020 at two commercial vineyards.
rows.notes: The study is in southwestern Idaho USA, not Chile; it uses wired radiometers with a neural-network reference temperature model and an edge-computing data logger, not a WSN with energy balance ET modeling. No water savings are reported (no comparison with conventional scheduling; Table 2 shows irrigation amounts were consistent across years) and no sugar or acidity data are presented. The 25% saving figure is not from this study.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report original multi-year field data from two vineyards.
rows.notes: No grape quality parameters (sugar, acidity) or yield were measured or reported; the study only reports CWSI, LWP, fASW and irrigation amounts (Fig. 7, Table 2). The system and location also differ from the WSN/energy-balance Chilean system described in the passage.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Table 2 report original four-year field data on CWSI and irrigation at two vineyards.
rows.notes: The study does report (Table 2, Section 4.4) that managers using the CWSI IoT DSS maintained consistent seasonal CWSI and irrigation amounts across four years with differing weather, which is loosely related to adapting irrigation to inter-annual climate variability, but it measures no resilience or productivity outcome and the system is not the WSN-plus-energy-balance system the passage refers to. Treated as no own evidence on the claimed effect; the study's own limitations section (4.5) notes the models may not perform outside the semiarid climatic range used for development (wind >5 m/s, low solar radiation, wet canopy).

notes: Full text appears complete. Primary field study of a CWSI-based IoT decision support system (in-situ infrared radiometers, neural-network reference temperature, edge computing, web pages) at two small vineyards in Idaho over 2017-2020. Outcomes reported are correlations between CWSI, LWP and fASW and consistency of seasonal CWSI and irrigation amounts; no yield, grape quality, water savings versus a control, or Chilean WSN/energy-balance data, so none of the five claims receives own-evidence support.
